quiz.q: Why write a custom error enum instead of just returning `Box<dyn Error>` everywhere?
options: Box<dyn Error> doesn't compile in stable Rust
A custom enum lets callers match on exactly which failure mode happened; Box<dyn Error> erases that distinction
Custom enums are faster at runtime
Box<dyn Error> can't be printed with Display
quiz.explain: Box<dyn Error> type-erases the concrete error, so a caller can only print it. A dedicated enum with one variant per failure mode lets callers `match` and react differently to each case.

quiz.q: What's the idiomatic shape of a custom error type for a function with multiple failure modes?
options: A single struct with a String message field
An enum with one variant per distinct way the operation can fail
A tuple of booleans, one per possible error
Reusing std::io::Error for every kind of failure
quiz.explain: One enum variant per failure mode keeps the caller's match meaningful — they can distinguish 'missing' from 'invalid' from any other case.

quiz.q: What is `impl std::fmt::Display` for on an error type?
options: It provides the {:?} Debug representation
It provides the {} representation — a human-readable message
It's required for the type to derive Debug
It converts the error into a Result
quiz.explain: Display gives the {} format — the human-facing message a user or log line would show, as opposed to Debug's {:?} which is for programmers.

quiz.q: What two traits does `std::error::Error` require as supertraits?
options: Clone and PartialEq
Debug and Display
Send and Sync
Copy and Default
quiz.explain: std::error::Error requires Debug + Display, which is why both need to be implemented (or derived, for Debug) before you can implement Error.

quiz.q: What does implementing `impl std::error::Error for MyError {}` (empty body) actually give you?
options: Nothing, the body must not be empty
It marks MyError as interoperable with the broader error-handling ecosystem — Box<dyn Error>, ? conversions, logging tools
It automatically derives Display for you
It disables the compiler's exhaustiveness checks
quiz.explain: Error has sensible defaults (source() returns None by default), so an empty impl block is valid and sufficient to make the type interoperate with code expecting `E: std::error::Error` or Box<dyn Error>.

options: It's required to derive Debug
So `?` can automatically convert a ParseIntError into MyError at any call site inside a function returning Result<_, MyError>
It lets you print the error with println!
It's needed to store the error in a Vec
quiz.explain: `?` calls From::from on the error it sees. Implementing From<ParseIntError> for MyError once means every `?` on a fallible parse call converts automatically, no .map_err needed.

quiz.q: What does the `source()` method on the `Error` trait provide?
options: The file and line number where the error occurred
A way to walk the underlying cause chain when your error wraps another error
The original input string that caused the error
A timestamp of when the error happened
quiz.explain: source() (default None) lets you expose a wrapped error, so callers/logging tools can print a full 'caused by' chain instead of just the top-level message.

quiz.q: A function returns `Result<u16, ConfigError>` and calls `text.parse()?` inside it, but there's no `From<ParseIntError> for ConfigError`. What happens?
options: It compiles, silently discarding the ParseIntError
Compile error — `?` has no way to convert ParseIntError into ConfigError
It compiles and panics at runtime instead
Rust automatically generates the From impl
quiz.explain: Without the From impl, `?` cannot convert the error type, so the compiler rejects the code with a type mismatch — the same rule from the ? operator lesson.

flashcards.front: What's the idiomatic shape of a custom error type with multiple failure modes?
flashcards.back: An enum with one variant per distinct failure mode — this keeps a caller's match meaningful, letting them distinguish and react to each case separately.

flashcards.front: What does Display give an error type, versus Debug?
flashcards.back: Display provides the {} representation — a human-readable message. Debug provides {:?} — a programmer-facing representation, usually just #[derive(Debug)].

flashcards.front: What two traits must an error type already implement before it can implement std::error::Error?
flashcards.back: Debug and Display — they're required supertraits of std::error::Error.

flashcards.front: Why implement std::error::Error even with an empty body?
flashcards.back: It makes your type interoperate with the broader error ecosystem: Box<dyn Error>, code generic over E: std::error::Error, and ?-conversions that rely on the Error trait.

flashcards.front: Why implement From<SourceError> for MyError instead of using .map_err() everywhere?
flashcards.back: Implement From once per source error type, and every `?` on that error type inside a function returning Result<_, MyError> converts automatically — no repeated .map_err(...) at each call site.

flashcards.front: What does the source() method on Error do, and what's its default?
flashcards.back: It exposes a wrapped/underlying error so callers can walk the cause chain. Its default implementation returns None; override it when your error variant wraps another error.

flashcards.front: Why is one giant catch-all error variant (e.g. Other(String)) a mistake?
flashcards.back: It defeats the purpose of a custom error type — callers can no longer match on which specific thing failed, they're back to just reading a message string.
